column4: Moses explicitly asks his Lord for a وَزِيرًا; this is the Quranic enactment of the source dictionary's burden-bearing helper.
Naming “Aaron, my brother” identifies the family member who will embody the requested minister in 20:29.
Moses asks that Aaron strengthen his أَزْرِي; this bodily support image is the source section's explicit parallel to a helper bracing one's back, while أزر is a distinct root from وزر.
“Make him share in my affair” states the partnership by which the minister takes part in his principal's task.
Moses gives abundant glorification as the purpose of receiving the helper: كَيْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيرًا.
Abundant remembrance completes the stated purpose of Aaron's support and links help, ease, and dhikr in the source image.
God says He appointed Aaron as a وَزِيرًا with Moses, directly answering the minister image with divine provision.
Moses asks for Aaron as a رِدْءًا who will confirm him, a precise nonlexical formulation of the supporting minister.
God answers, “We shall strengthen your arm through your brother,” turning fraternal aid into the same bodily support image as the braced back.
Allah, Gabriel, and the righteous believers stand with the Prophet, and the angels are a ظَهِيرٌ; this directly realizes the source dictionary's “back” as helper.
Moses vows never to be a ظَهِيرًا for criminals, marking the moral boundary on whom one's supporting back may uphold.
The human cry “Where is the escape?” opens the exact refuge scene answered by لَا وَزَرَ in 75:11.
لَا وَزَرَ uses the same و ز ر root in its “mountain/refuge” sense and denies any such shelter on the Last Day.
إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ names the Lord as the only final destination immediately after refuge is denied, exactly joining the section's source root and closing direction.
The three discover that there is no مَلْجَأَ from Allah except to Him, the paradoxical refuge-in-the-One-from-whom-one-cannot-flee developed by the section.
“Flee to Allah” turns the refuge image into a command of directed flight, matching the section's movement toward the Lord.
Moses first asks his Lord to expand his breast, beginning the sequence that the source section aligns with surah 94 before the request for a minister.
“Ease my affair” supplies the second step of the breast–ease–minister–remembrance sequence developed in the source prose.
God's “You have been granted your request, Moses” confirms that the Lord supplies the requested ease and helper.
God sends Moses and his brother together and tells them not to slacken in His remembrance, joining granted partnership to the prayer's dhikr purpose.
Moses' constricted breast and speech difficulty lead directly to “send for Aaron,” restaging the need from which the supporting brother is requested.
God answers the request by sending both brothers with His signs and assuring them of His hearing presence, so divine support underwrites human partnership.
Moses appoints Aaron as his deputy among the people and commands him to set matters right, a functional minister scene that also activates the source definition of rabb as one who reforms.
They carry their أَوْزَارَهُمْ on their ظُهُورِهِمْ, placing the source section's burden and back together in one literalized judgment scene.
The Messenger “puts off them” their burden and shackles, closely matching the source section's وَضَعْنَا عَنكَ relation even though the noun here is إصر.
One who turns from the Reminder will carry a وِزْرًا on Resurrection Day, preserving the source root's burden sense and its bearer relation.
The burden of 20:100 remains with them, and this ayah calls it an evil load on Resurrection Day; it completes what that wizr does to its bearer.
حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا joins “laying down” with the same burden root, an exact lexical echo in the distinct idiom of war ending.
The prayer asks God not to lay on the believers an إِصْرًا, not to make them carry what exceeds capacity, and ends “You are our protector”; burden relief and refuge meet in one appeal.
God makes mountain shelters and protective garments for people, uniquely joining the source dictionary's mountain-refuge and girded-garment branches in one ayah.
The youths take refuge in the cave and ask their Lord to grant mercy and prepare right conduct in their affair, joining mountain shelter, Lordward prayer, and a made-fit task.
Retreat to the cave is followed by the promise that the Lord will spread mercy and prepare مِرْفَقًا in their affair, making divine shelter also practical facilitation.
In the cave the Prophet is told not to grieve because Allah is with the two, after which divine tranquility and unseen forces support him.
God places no hardship in the religion and commands believers to hold fast to Him, then names Himself their excellent Protector and Helper; relief and refuge are inseparable here.
“Remember the name of your Lord” and devote yourself wholly to Him gives the Lordward remembrance for which Moses sought supporting partnership.
The next ayah identifies the Lord of east and west and commands, “take Him as guardian,” making reliance the consequence of the remembrance in 73:8.
“Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?” states the source section's reversal plainly: the Lord bears up the servant rather than needing a minister.
Allah is sufficient for the Prophet and is the One who strengthened him with divine victory and the believers, combining the true support with human supporters.
The Prophet is told to declare Allah sufficient, trust in Him, and name Him Lord of the mighty Throne, a direct stance of reliance on the sovereign Lord.
Allah is the مَوْلَى of the believers whereas the rejecters have no protector, defining the Lord–servant relation through active protection.
Whoever relies upon Allah finds Him sufficient, directly expressing the minister image's dependence and shelter with God as its true object.
God's forgiveness of the Prophet's earlier and later fault and completion of favor is a concrete same-addressee instance of the Lord removing what weighs upon His servant.
God promises the Prophet a mighty support immediately after forgiveness and completed favor, joining burden relief to divine backing.
The same divine speaker reminds the Prophet that He found him an orphan and gave shelter, a direct instance of the Lord as the servant's refuge.
God acknowledges that the Prophet's breast is constricted by what opponents say, providing a precise reversal against the opened breast in surah 94.
The answer to the constricted breast of 15:97 is to glorify the Lord with praise and prostrate, linking strain to the same Lordward tasbih sought in Moses' prayer.
The Prophet is told to endure his Lord's judgment because he is “before Our eyes,” then to glorify his Lord; protection and tasbih occur in one address.
The arrival of Allah's help supplies the enabling support whose response is glorification in 110:3.
After divine help and victory, the Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord and seek forgiveness, echoing support ordered toward tasbih.
Shuayb seeks only reform, says his success is through Allah, relies on Him, and turns to Him; this concretely unites the source definitions of reformer, reliance, and Lordward direction.
The Prophet is told to consult companions in the affair, but after deciding to rely on Allah, distinguishing valued human counsel from ultimate dependence on the Lord.
The queen asks her chiefs for counsel and refuses to decide an affair without their presence, exactly staging the source definition of a ruler relying on advisers' judgment.
The Messenger says no one can protect him from Allah and he can find no مُلْتَحَدًا apart from Him, closely paralleling the section's no-refuge-except-to-Him claim.
No one can alter the Lord's words, and the addressee will find no مُلْتَحَدًا apart from Him; the Lord is the sole refuge.
Allah, rather than feared human enemies, is the believers' Protector and the best of helpers, directly naming the source image's true supporting master.
If opponents turn away, believers are reminded that Allah is their Protector, “excellent Protector and excellent Helper.”

“No burden-bearer bears another's burden” sets the accountability boundary against the source dictionary's minister who voluntarily carries his principal's load; the ayah also ends with return to the Lord.
Each person's guidance or error falls on that person and no bearer carries another's burden, limiting the helper metaphor in moral judgment.
A heavily laden soul may call even a close relative to its load, yet none of it is carried; this is the sharpest reversal of the kin-minister who takes another's weight.
No bearer carries another's burden and all return to their Lord, placing nontransferable accountability beside the section's Lordward destination.
The scrolls of Moses and Abraham affirm that no bearer bears another's burden, a scriptural boundary on the Moses–Aaron minister image.
Misleaders bear their own burdens and some burdens arising from those they mislead; this qualifies nontransfer by moral causation rather than a helper taking guilt away.
Rejecters promise believers, “We will carry your sins,” but the ayah denies that they can carry any of them, exposing a false offer to act as burden-bearer.
The misleaders will bear their own loads and further loads with them, showing acquired responsibility for misleading rather than substitution for another bearer.
Noah's son says he will seek refuge on a mountain that will protect him, but no protector exists from God's command except His mercy; the dictionary's refuge-mountain is explicitly overruled.
The expelled people thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah, but their constructed refuge failed from an unexpected direction.
Death overtakes people even inside lofty fortified towers, setting a limit on every material shelter named by the source's broad refuge definition.
The command to answer the Lord precedes a day with no مَلْجَإٍ, matching the Last-Day denial of refuge while directing response to God.
For the appointed reckoning the wrongdoers will find no مَوْئِلًا, another explicit denial of refuge in judgment.
False gods own no share in creation and God has no ظَهِيرٍ among them, denying that the sovereign Lord requires the kind of supporting minister a ruler needs.
The Prophet praises the King who has no partner in rule and no protecting ally arising from weakness, explicitly rejecting neediness in the divine sovereign.
The rejecter is a ظَهِيرًا against his Lord, turning the supporting-back relation toward the wrong side.
The Prophet is commanded not to be a ظَهِيرًا for the rejecters, repeating the ethical boundary on support found in Moses' vow.
Shuayb asks whether his clan is mightier than Allah and rebukes his people for putting God behind their backs, reversing the back as a place of relied-upon support.
God says He never took the misleaders as an عَضُدًا, an arm-support image that denies any need for corrupt helpers and parallels the arm strengthened in 28:35.
No one can shield people from Allah if He intends harm or withhold His mercy, and they find no protector or helper apart from Him.
Taking protectors besides Allah is compared to the spider taking a house, the frailty of the shelter exposing false refuge.
The garden owner has no company to support him apart from Allah and cannot defend himself, showing worldly backing collapse at the point of need.
Korah has no faction to help him against Allah and cannot help himself when the earth swallows him, a failed human “back.”
People take gods besides Allah hoping to be helped, locating the error precisely in seeking support from false masters.
Those gods cannot help their devotees; instead the devotees are mustered as troops for them, reversing who supports whom.
The question asks what army could help anyone besides the Merciful, denying an alternative body of supporters.
On the Day, no patron can avail another and none are helped except those shown mercy, bounding interpersonal support by the Lord's mercy.
Neither parent can avail child nor child parent before the Lord, contrasting the effective brotherly aid of Aaron with kinship's limit in final accountability.
On that Day a person flees from his brother, a pointed reversal of Moses seeking his brother as his supporting minister.
A mountain would humble and split if the Quran descended upon it, unsettling the mountain's appearance as an unshakable refuge or bearer.
The heavens, earth, and mountains shrink from bearing the Trust, while the human undertakes it; the scene tests what can carry a weight rather than merely shelter from it.
God facilitates the miserly denier toward hardship, the dark counterpart to divinely granted ease in Moses' prayer and surah 94.
The shared word calls people not to take one another as arbāb apart from Allah, setting the boundary between human masters and the true Lord.
No prophet commands people to take angels or prophets as lords, excluding exalted servants from the master's place.
Taking scholars and monks as lords besides Allah exemplifies the source dictionary's “obeyed master” sense misdirected toward creatures.
Joseph contrasts divided human lords with Allah, the One and Overpowering, making the lexical master sense a theological choice.
Rule belongs only to Allah and worship is commanded for Him alone, explaining why creaturely masters cannot occupy the final refuge of the source image.
Pharaoh's claim “I am your highest lord” is the tyrant's counterfeit of the master-title that belongs to God.
The request to untie the knot from Moses' tongue supplies the limitation that makes Aaron's greater eloquence and confirming support in 28:34 intelligible.
Moses asks that people understand his speech, completing the speech problem immediately before he requests a minister.
Moses tells his Lord that his breast tightens and his tongue does not flow, grounding the request for Aaron in 26:13.
Moses fears retaliation for an earlier offense; this ayah adds danger, beyond speech difficulty, to his need for divine and fraternal support.
Moses recalls killing one of Pharaoh's people and fears being killed, the concrete peril immediately preceding his request for Aaron as support.
God sends both Moses and Aaron to the denying people, showing the shared mission for which the minister of 25:35 was appointed.
Giving Moses his brother Aaron as a prophet “from Our mercy” presents the supportive brother as a divine gift, though it does not call him minister here.
God's favor is explicitly bestowed on Moses and Aaron together, framing their partnership as provision from the Lord.
God rescues both brothers and their people from great distress, continuing the Lord's supporting action toward the paired servants.
God helps Moses and Aaron until they prevail, making divine aid the ground of the brothers' successful shared mission.
The people say they were made to carry أَوْزَارًا of ornaments and then cast them, a physical-load use of the source root distinct from moral burden.
The Messenger bears what he is charged with and the audience bears what it is charged with, assigning each party's task without transferring it.
God will cast a “weighty word” upon the Prophet, a specific counterpoint to the burden He removes and the task He eases.
The donkey carrying books is a bearer that gains nothing from its load, a negative boundary on equating mere load-carrying with the purposeful help of a minister.
Even if humans and jinn were ظَهِيرًا to one another, they could not produce the Quran's like; the helper word is used for total mutual backing.
The Israelites “support one another” in sin and aggression against part of their own people, an unethical collective form of the source's backing relation.
Faithfulness to treaty partners is conditioned on their not supporting anyone against the believers, showing support as an alliance-defining act.
The People of the Book who backed the confederates are brought down from their fortresses, joining wrongful support with a failed stronghold.
Those who support others in expelling believers are placed outside permitted allegiance, another moral boundary on whom one backs.
The opponents call Moses' and Aaron's revelations “two sorceries supporting one another,” preserving the root's mutual-backing sense inside hostile speech.
A crop's shoot strengthens it—فَآزَرَهُ—giving a concrete Quranic image for the separate أ ز ر root used in Moses' “strengthen my back,” not the و ز ر burden root.
The hypocrites would bolt toward a refuge, caves, or any entrance if they found one, a physical flight-to-shelter scene without the source section's Lordward correction.
The chiefs offer strength and force but leave the command to the queen, completing 27:32's ruler-and-counsellors scene while preserving her authority.
The king reserves Joseph for himself and declares him established and trusted, a functional court analogue to the dependable adviser in the source definition of minister.
Joseph asks to be placed over the land's storehouses, specifying the entrusted public burden that follows his admission to the king's confidence.
The believers conduct their affair by mutual consultation, paralleling both counsel relied upon and Moses' request that Aaron share in his affair.
Joseph uses rabb for the cupbearer's human master, directly exemplifying the source dictionary's nondivine “master” sense.
“Mention me to your lord” again uses rabb for the royal master and places a close court servant between a petitioner and the ruler.
The command “return to your lord” uses rabb for the king, another clear Quranic instance of the title's human-master sense.
Pharaoh says to Moses, “Did we not rear you among us as a child?”; نُرَبِّكَ activates the root's nurture and setting-right sense while exposing a tyrant's claim on the servant.
The prayer for parents recalls “as they reared me when small,” a creaturely instance of the nurturing sense behind the source definition of rabb as reformer.
Calling God “Owner of dominion” distinguishes the absolute sovereign from rulers whose authority and burdens are granted and removed by Him.
God desires to lighten the human burden because the human was created weak, a direct statement of the Lord's relieving action.
God explicitly lightens the believers' obligation after knowing their weakness, showing the master adjusting the servant's load.
God charges no soul beyond what He has given it and promises ease after hardship, combining measured burden with the promise central to surah 94.
God tells the Prophet, “We shall ease you toward ease,” a same-addressee promise of divine facilitation.
The generous, God-fearing believer is facilitated toward ease, showing ease as a divinely prepared course.
In the fasting ruling God explicitly desires ease rather than hardship for people, a legal instance of the Lord easing a duty.
God knows the community cannot sustain the full night measure, turns toward them, and repeatedly permits whatever recitation is easy, concretely reducing a devotional load.
“We made the Quran easy for remembrance” joins the two successive aims in Moses' prayer—ease and dhikr—in one repeated formula.
The repeated claim that the Quran is made easy for remembrance reinforces facilitation as a means to remembering God.
This third refrain again links what God makes easy with the human act of taking reminder.
The final refrain preserves the surah-wide repetition of divinely made ease for remembrance.
God says He made revelation easy in the Prophet's tongue so he can give good news and warning, meeting Moses' requests for eased speech and effective mission.
The Quran is made easy in the Prophet's tongue so that people may remember, again joining eased utterance to remembrance.
After Zechariah's prayer is answered, he is told to remember his Lord much and glorify morning and evening; a granted request likewise issues in abundant remembrance and tasbih.
Believers are commanded to remember Allah with abundant remembrance, the same stated purpose for which Moses asks a supporting brother.
They are also commanded to glorify Him morning and evening, completing the dhikr–tasbih pair begun in 33:41.
“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High” directs the same praise toward the Lord to whom the servant finally turns.

Clothing that covers nakedness supplies a plausible Quranic garment counterpart to the source dictionary's ittizār or tied waistcloth branch, though the ayah uses neither the garment form nor the و ز ر root.
When the two groups come into view, Moses' companions think they have been overtaken; this is the crisis of failed outward escape answered by reliance on the Lord in 26:62.
Moses rejects despair because “my Lord is with me; He will guide me,” making the Lord Himself the support when no visible refuge remains.
The Prophet is commanded to seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak, directly joining the act of taking shelter to rabb, the section's closing title.
The command to seek refuge in the Lord of humankind is an exact Lordward refuge stance.
“King of humankind” immediately explains the sovereign-master dimension of the Rabb invoked as refuge in 114:1.
Allah is declared sufficient for the Prophet and for the believers who follow him, another same-addressee statement that the Lord supplies His servants' support.
“To your Lord is the final end” repeats the section's exact Lordward direction and presents Him as the terminus after all other recourse ends.
Later in the same refuge-denying surah, “to your Lord that day is the driving” restates the unavoidable destination first named in 75:12.
“To your Lord is the return” repeats the section's closing direction while correcting the human illusion of self-sufficiency in the preceding ayat.
The human is described as laboring toward the Lord until meeting Him, joining strenuous work to the Lordward direction that follows work in surah 94.
The reassured soul is commanded to return to its Lord, a fulfilled and peaceful form of the section's final turning.
God tells the Prophet that the Quran was not sent down to make him suffer, a same-addressee denial that the Lord's revelation is meant as a crushing load.
Those who gave refuge and support are paired with the emigrants as mutual protectors, combining shelter and active backing in one community relation.
The repeated description “gave refuge and supported” makes hospitality and help the defining action of true believers.
Jesus asks who will be his helpers toward Allah and the disciples volunteer, a prophetic-mission parallel to Moses requesting a human supporter for God's work.
Believers are told to be helpers of Allah as Jesus' disciples were; the supported party then becomes ظَاهِرِينَ, linking aid to the root's distinct prevailing sense.
“If you support Allah, He will support you and make your feet firm” sets creaturely service and divine strengthening in a reciprocal relation.
Two messengers are reinforced with a third when rejected, a precise narrative instance of adding a person to brace a difficult mission.
God answers the believers' plea for help by reinforcing them with successive angels, an enacted parallel to the angelic support named in 66:4.
Thamud carve houses from the mountains while feeling secure, a direct Quranic realization of the mountain as protective shelter.
The Prophet is taught to say, “My Lord, I seek refuge in You” from the devils' incitements, joining the refuge act explicitly to Rabb.
He also seeks refuge in his Lord from the devils' very presence, completing the two-part shelter prayer.
The Prophet is told that flight will not benefit anyone fleeing death or killing, placing a limit on escape as refuge.
The death from which people flee will inevitably meet them, another direct boundary on physical escape.
On the day people turn in flight, they have no protector from Allah; the attempted escape ends without a human or material backer.
When Allah intends harm for a people it cannot be repelled, and they have no protecting patron apart from Him.
The dominion of heavens and earth belongs to Allah, and no protector or helper exists apart from Him; sovereignty and exclusive refuge meet explicitly.
Allah owns the heavens and earth, gives life and death, and people have no protector or helper apart from Him.
Humans cannot escape in the earth and have no protector or helper apart from Allah, combining failed flight with failed backing.
If the rejecters fought, they would turn their backs and find neither protector nor helper, making the physical back part of the failure of support.
The question asks whether they possess gods that can protect them from God, then denies those gods can help themselves or enjoy His protection.
Those invoked apart from Allah can neither help their callers nor help themselves, exposing false supporters' incapacity.
Abel tells his aggressor that he will bear both the sin against him and his own sin, a moral-causation exception that clarifies how one person's act can add to another's load without substitution.

Joseph seeks refuge in Allah when solicited; his following use of rabb has a known master/Lord ambiguity, so the ayah also exposes the human-master and divine-Lord senses without safely collapsing them.
After ablution rules, God says He does not intend hardship but purification, a concrete legal instance of the Lord refusing an onerous load.
In allocating parents' nursing and maintenance duties, the ayah says no soul is charged beyond its capacity, a specific boundary on assigned family burdens.
The command concerning an orphan's property and just measure is qualified by charging no soul beyond capacity, limiting what the Master requires.
The promise to believing doers is introduced by the rule that no soul is charged beyond capacity, another repeated formulation of measured obligation.
God charges no soul beyond capacity and keeps a truthful record, combining a bounded load with exact accountability.
Thamud carve homes in the mountains after being settled in the land, another mountain-as-habitation scene, though refuge from an immediate threat is not stated.
The people skillfully carve houses from mountains, repeating the built mountain shelter but without 15:82's explicit security term.
Moses seeks refuge in “my Lord and your Lord” from every arrogant person who denies reckoning, adding his own explicit Lordward refuge stance.
When satanic provocation comes, the addressee is commanded to seek refuge in Allah, turning spiritual attack into the same action of flight to divine shelter.
The repeated instruction to seek refuge in Allah from satanic incitement presents God as the immediate protector in an inward threat.
Before reciting the Quran the addressee is commanded to seek refuge in Allah from Satan, placing refuge at the threshold of the weighty revealed word.
Mary seeks refuge in the Merciful from the unknown visitor, a concrete human-threat scene of taking divine shelter.
Mary's mother entrusts her and her offspring to God's refuge from Satan, extending protection to one who cannot yet seek it herself.
The command to cooperate in righteousness but not in sin gives an explicit ethical rule for when people should or should not act as one another's support.
Dhu al-Qarnayn asks the people to help him with strength in building the barrier, a leader sharing a difficult public task with supporters.
Pharaoh asks his chiefs what they advise regarding Moses, staging a ruler's reliance on a council, albeit within a hostile cause.
The chiefs recommend delaying Moses and Aaron and gathering magicians, supplying the counsel requested by the ruler in 26:35.
Women are told to draw their outer garments around themselves so they may be recognized and not harmed, a protective-clothing parallel to the source's girded-garment branch.
The Prophet asks whether reinforcement by three thousand angels will suffice the believers, a specific angelic-backing scene.
Steadfastness and reverence are answered with a promise of five thousand marked angels, completing the offered reinforcement.
The Prophet is told to endure hostile speech and glorify his Lord throughout the day, another strain-to-tasbih movement in the same surah as Moses' minister prayer.
The Prophet is commanded to remember the name of his Lord morning and evening, matching the remembrance enabled by Moses' requested support.
Night prostration and prolonged glorification complete the remembrance-and-tasbih pair begun in 76:25.
Night glorification continues the protected tasbih command of 52:48 and completes that passage's temporal scope.
